proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(n\ge1\), \(s\in[1,2]\), \(M\ge2\),
\(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\), and any measurable connected interval rule
\(I_n\) satisfying the honesty constraint in \(\text{def:minimax-length}\).
Write
\[
 a=1-\alpha,
 \qquad p_s=2+\frac1s=\frac{2s+1}{s},
 \qquad C_b=2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s},
\]
and put \(T_n=n\kappa_n^{p_s}\),
\(B_n=\sqrt{C_bT_n}\), and \(\beta=p_s/2=(2s+1)/(2s)\).
The constant \(C_b\) is finite and strictly positive because the fixed,
nonzero bump \(\psi\) has \(0<H_s<\infty\), while \(M\ge2\).

We first integrate the fixed-cutoff continuum.  By
\(\text{prop:fixed-cutoff-bump-membership-kl}\), for every
\(u\in[-1,1]\), both \(Q_u\) and \(Q_0\) belong to \(\mathcal P_n\),
their effect labels are \(u\) and \(0\), respectively, and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 &\le\left\{C_b n(\kappa_n|u|)^{p_s}\right\}^{1/2}\\
 &=\sqrt{C_bn\kappa_n^{p_s}}\,|u|^{p_s/2}\\
 &=B_n|u|^\beta.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The middle equality uses \(\kappa_n>0\), and the last equality uses the
definitions of \(T_n\), \(B_n\), and \(\beta\).  Honesty at \(Q_u\)
and the defining variational inequality for total variation give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{u\in I_n\}
 &\ge Q_u^{\otimes n}\{u\in I_n\}
      -\operatorname{TV}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})\\
 &\ge a-B_n|u|^\beta.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since a probability is nonnegative,
\[
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{u\in I_n\}
 \ge[a-B_n|u|^\beta]_+.
 \tag{1}
\]

For completeness, the integration in \((1)\) can be justified without
assuming any unmentioned set-valued Fubini theorem.  For \(m\ge1\), let
\(u_j=-1+2j/m\), \(j=0,\ldots,m\).  Every connected subset
\(J\subseteq[-1,1]\) satisfies
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^m\mathbf 1\{u_j\in J\}\le1+\frac m2|J|,
\]
because grid points in a nonempty interval from its first to its last
occupy consecutive positions separated by \(2/m\); the inequality is
also immediate when \(J\) is empty.  Thus, pointwise,
\[
 |I_n|\ge\frac2m\sum_{j=0}^m\mathbf 1\{u_j\in I_n\}-\frac2m.
\]
Taking \(Q_0\)-expectations, applying \((1)\), and letting
\(m\to\infty\) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_{Q_0}|I_n|
 &\ge\int_{-1}^1[a-B_n|u|^\beta]_+\,du\\
 &=2\int_0^1[a-B_nu^\beta]_+\,du\\
 &=F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n).
 \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The limit is a Riemann-sum limit because
\(u\mapsto[a-B_n|u|^\beta]_+\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\).
Since \(Q_0\in\mathcal P_n\), \((2)\) implies
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n|\ge F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n).
\]
Taking the infimum over all honest connected interval rules in
\(\text{def:minimax-length}\) proves
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
\]
for every \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\).

We next evaluate the integral.  If \(B_n\le a\), the positive part is
inactive on \([0,1]\), so
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
 &=2\int_0^1(a-B_nu^\beta)\,du\\
 &=2a-\frac{2B_n}{\beta+1}\\
 &=2a-\frac{4s}{4s+1}B_n,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where \(\beta+1=(4s+1)/(2s)\).  If \(B_n>a\), the integrand is
positive exactly for \(0\le u<u_0\), where
\[
 u_0=\left(\frac a{B_n}\right)^{1/\beta}
 =\left(\frac a{B_n}\right)^{2s/(2s+1)}.
\]
Since \(B_nu_0^\beta=a\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
 &=2\left(au_0-\frac{B_nu_0^{\beta+1}}{\beta+1}\right)\\
 &=2au_0\left(1-\frac1{\beta+1}\right)\\
 &=\frac{2a(2s+1)}{4s+1}
   \left(\frac a{B_n}\right)^{2s/(2s+1)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This proves the two-piece formula asserted in
\(\text{def:integrated-fixed-cutoff-lower-function}\).

Suppose now that \(\kappa_n\le1/16\).  By
\(\text{prop:moving-cutoff-membership-kl}\), every \(P_t\) belongs to
\(\mathcal P_n\), has effect label \(t\), and obeys
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \le4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
\]
Repeating the honesty transfer and the connected-grid integration used
above, now with \(t\) in place of \(u\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_{P_0}|I_n|
 &\ge\int_{-1}^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}]_+\,dt\\
 &=2\int_0^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_nt}]_+\,dt\\
 &=G_\alpha(\tau_n).
 \tag{3}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Because \(P_0\in\mathcal P_n\), taking the infimum as before proves
\(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge G_\alpha(\tau_n)\).  Combining this with
\((2)\) proves
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge\max\{G_\alpha(\tau_n),F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\}.
\]
To evaluate \((3)\), if \(\tau_n\le a^2/16\), the integrand is
nonnegative throughout \([0,1]\), and
\[
 2\int_0^1(a-4\sqrt{\tau_nt})\,dt
 =2a-\frac{16}{3}\sqrt{\tau_n}.
\]
If \(\tau_n>a^2/16\), its positive region ends at
\(t_0=a^2/(16\tau_n)\), and therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 2\int_0^{t_0}(a-4\sqrt{\tau_nt})\,dt
 &=2\left(at_0-\frac83\sqrt{\tau_n}t_0^{3/2}\right)\\
 &=\frac{a^3}{24\tau_n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This is the asserted formula for \(G_\alpha\).

We retain the coarse fixed-cutoff comparison as an immediate consequence
of the sharper function \(F_{\alpha,s,M}\).  Define
\[
 D_{s,M,\alpha}
 =\frac{2a(2s+1)}{4s+1}
   a^{2s/(2s+1)}C_b^{-s/(2s+1)}>0,
 \qquad
 c_{\mathrm{fix}}=\min\{a,D_{s,M,\alpha}\}>0.
\]
If \(B_n\le a\), then \(4s/(4s+1)<1\), whence
\[
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
 =2a-\frac{4s}{4s+1}B_n\ge a.
\]
If \(B_n>a\), the second branch and
\(1/p_s=s/(2s+1)\) give
\[
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
 =D_{s,M,\alpha}T_n^{-1/p_s}.
\]
Consequently, in both cases,
\[
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)
 \ge c_{\mathrm{fix}}\min\{1,T_n^{-1/p_s}\}.
 \tag{4}
\]
The definitions of \(T_n\), \(p_s\), and \(\rho_n\) imply
\[
 T_n^{-1/p_s}
 =(n\kappa_n^{p_s})^{-1/p_s}
 =\frac{n^{-s/(2s+1)}}{\kappa_n}
 =\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}.
\]
Combining this identity, \((2)\), and \((4)\) proves the claimed
fixed-cutoff inequality.

It remains to combine the two sources of difficulty.  For every
\(\tau>0\), the explicit formula for \(G_\alpha\) implies
\[
 G_\alpha(\tau)\ge c_{\mathrm{loc}}\min\{1,\tau^{-1}\},
 \qquad c_{\mathrm{loc}}=\frac{a^3}{24}>0.
 \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, on \(0<\tau\le a^2/16\), the first branch is at least
\(2a/3\ge a^3/24\).  On \(a^2/16<\tau\le1\), the second branch is at
least \(a^3/24\); and on \(\tau>1\), it equals
\(a^3/(24\tau)\).  Here \(0<a<1\), by \(0<\alpha<1/4\).

Put
\[
 A_n=\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n},
 \qquad R_n=\frac1{n\kappa_n^3}=\tau_n^{-1}.
\]
When \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), inequalities \((4)\) and \((5)\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 &\ge\max\{c_{\mathrm{fix}}\min(1,A_n),
              c_{\mathrm{loc}}\min(1,R_n)\}\\
 &\ge\frac12\min\{c_{\mathrm{fix}},c_{\mathrm{loc}}\}
       \{\min(1,A_n)+\min(1,R_n)\}\\
 &\ge\frac12\min\{c_{\mathrm{fix}},c_{\mathrm{loc}}\}
       \min(1,A_n+R_n)\\
 &=\frac12\min\{c_{\mathrm{fix}},c_{\mathrm{loc}}\}r_n.
 \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate inequality follows by considering whether
\(A_n+R_n\le1\): in that case both individual truncations are inactive,
whereas otherwise their sum is at least one.

Finally, suppose \(1/16<\kappa_n\le1/8\).  Since
\(n\rho_n=n^{(s+1)/(2s+1)}\ge1\),
\[
 \frac{R_n}{A_n}
 =\frac1{n\kappa_n^2\rho_n}
 <\frac{256}{n\rho_n}
 \le256.
\]
Thus \(R_n\le256A_n\), and
\[
 r_n=\min(1,A_n+R_n)\le257\min(1,A_n).
 \tag{7}
\]
For \(A_n<1\), this follows from
\(A_n+R_n\le257A_n\); for \(A_n\ge1\), it follows from
\(r_n\le1\le257\min(1,A_n)\).  The fixed-cutoff bound and \((7)\)
therefore imply
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge\frac{c_{\mathrm{fix}}}{257}r_n.
\]
Taking
\[
 C_{\mathrm{low}}
 =\min\left\{
 \frac12\min(c_{\mathrm{fix}},c_{\mathrm{loc}}),
 \frac{c_{\mathrm{fix}}}{257}
 \right\}>0
\]
proves the all-strength lower comparison.  Every constant depends only
on \(s\), \(M\), and \(\alpha\), as required.

proposed.name: F_{\alpha,s,M}
proposed.construction:
Put \(p_s=2+1/s\) and
\[
 C_b=2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}.
\]
For \(T\ge0\), put \(B(T)=\sqrt{C_bT}\) and define
\[
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T)
 =2\int_0^1\left[1-\alpha-B(T)u^{p_s/2}\right]_+\,du.
\]
Writing \(a=1-\alpha\), the same function has the explicit representation
\[
 F_{\alpha,s,M}(T)
 =\begin{cases}
 2a-\dfrac{4s}{4s+1}B(T),& B(T)\le a,\\[6pt]
 \dfrac{2a(2s+1)}{4s+1}
 \left\{\dfrac{a}{B(T)}\right\}^{2s/(2s+1)},&B(T)>a.
 \end{cases}
\]
At \(T=0\), the first branch applies and gives \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(0)=2(1-\alpha)\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: This definition records the exact integral and its evaluated two-piece form, with the constant inherited from the already-proved fixed-cutoff total-variation inequality.

proposed.comparator_claim: Their unknown-threshold result transfers the minimax rate for estimating a sharp-RD discontinuity location from a convolution white-noise model.
Their moderate-break analysis derives a Gaussian-process limit experiment and a nearly weighted-average-power maximizing test.
Their Theorem 1 gives uniformly asymptotically valid conditional tests with a functional nuisance parameter.
Their Theorem 1 shows that risk functions attainable in the weak-GMM Gaussian-process experiment bound finite-sample asymptotic risk.
Their Theorem 3.1 characterizes optimal one-sided confidence intervals through an ordered modulus over convex fixed-index regression classes.
Their sharp testable implications for fuzzy-RD validity are inequalities in the joint outcome--treatment distribution at the cutoff.
Their LoTTA model propagates posterior uncertainty about an unknown cutoff into fuzzy-RD effect estimation.
Their main unknown-discontinuity theory treats testing and estimation in sharp RD, with fuzzy RD discussed separately.

prose_updates.tldr: For fuzzy regression discontinuity with a weak compliance jump and unknown cutoff, cutoff recovery and causal-effect informativeness are distinct. Integrating the moving-cutoff continuum gives the explicit lower value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), while integrating the causal-valid fixed-cutoff bump continuum gives the new exact envelope \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\). Thus \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\) at every declared strength, \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge\max\{G_\alpha(\tau_n),F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\}\) when \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), and \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\) globally under the unchanged binary H{\"o}lder-margin class. Finite-grid four-cell calibration remains valid for every compatible treatment--outcome association, including singular cells. The support-wide profile upper bound, attainment, the \(s=1\) finite-positive critical decision value, and full-model least favorability remain open.

project_justification.gap: Known-cutoff weak-fuzzy inference, sharp-RD unknown-cutoff rates, generic weak-identification decision theory, and Bayesian propagation of cutoff uncertainty have been developed separately. None supplies the two integrated label-wise lower envelopes, an all-strength minimax converse, and an attaining honest connected interval when the cutoff and fuzzy denominator weaken jointly; the lower side is proved here, whereas attainment remains open.
project_justification.niche: The preserved binary uniform-design class makes two complementary causal lifts explicit while leaving the observable treatment--outcome association unrestricted. The moving-cutoff continuum measures slope-location ambiguity through \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), and the fixed-cutoff compact-bump continuum measures ordinary nonparametric jump difficulty through \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\).
project_justification.fill: The project integrates both legal continua to prove \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\) throughout the strength shell, the maximum of \(F_{\alpha,s,M}\) and \(G_\alpha\) on the moving-family range, and the coarse all-strength converse \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\). It also defines a support-wide four-cell profile and proves exact finite-grid calibration while leaving association free. The matching upper frontier, complete critical experiment, exact finite-positive decision values, and a total attaining interval remain unresolved.

prose_updates.related_work: Hahn, Todd, and van der Klaauw (2001) supply the local Wald identification argument. Feir, Lemieux, and Marmer (2016) and Noack and Rothe (2024, Theorem 1) give weak-identification-robust inference at a fixed known cutoff; they inform the exact singleton-cutoff finite-grid calibration and reduction proved here, but no first-order residual-jump equivalence is claimed. The integrated fixed-cutoff bump continuum sharpens the lower analysis to the explicit value function \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\), while the moving-cutoff continuum supplies the distinct \(1/(n\kappa_n^3)\) difficulty and explicit value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\). Porter and Yu (2015, Sections 3--5) and Tuvaandorj (2020, Sections 3--4) study unknown-location behavior predominantly in sharp designs, without this weak causal ratio or connected honest-length criterion. Elliott and M{\"u}ller (2014, Sections 2.1--2.3) motivate process experiments for moderate unknown breaks, but do not solve the present H{\"o}lder-margin decision problem. Andrews and Mikusheva (2016, Theorem 1) and Andrews and Mikusheva (2022, Theorem 1 and Section 4) inform nuisance calibration and weak-decision analysis; Armstrong and Koles{\'a}r (2018, Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.4) connect testing power to expected length over convex fixed-index classes. None proves the still-open support-wide profile upper bound over the translated nonconvex union. Arai, Hsu, Kitagawa, Mourifi{\'e}, and Wan (2022, Section 2) motivate retaining the full joint outcome--treatment law. Kowalska, van de Wiel, and van der Pas (2025 version, Sections 3 and 6) propagate unknown-cutoff uncertainty in a Bayesian model without uniform frequentist honesty or minimax length.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: A product of the two marginal Bernoulli likelihoods is not the likelihood of the observed pair when association is unrestricted. The finite-grid calibration therefore uses the complete binned four-cell vector and a method-of-types threshold that remains valid on singular cell faces. Its dimension cost \(\zeta_n\) need not be negligible on every sequence satisfying cutoff recovery; \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\) is only the proposed domain for a conservative finite-grid upper-rate comparison, and no profile upper rate has yet been proved there. Separately, an untruncated second moment of a translated-cutoff mixture does not determine a critical constant; boundary truncation, mixture renormalization, the signed effect label, and second-order centering must remain in the experiment.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The model has no outcome-variance, null-residual-variance, covariance-eigenvalue, or joint-cell positivity floor, and the strengthened lower bound adds none. The proved lower results include the moving-cutoff causal lift and its Kullback--Leibler bound, the explicit integrated value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), the fixed-cutoff compact-bump causal lift and its \(n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}\) divergence bound, the exact integrated fixed-cutoff envelope \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\), and the all-strength converse \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\). Exact singleton-cutoff finite-grid four-cell calibration and population false-split separation are also proved uniformly over permitted binary treatment--outcome associations. These facts do not establish continuum honesty, an upper expected-length rate, or attainment by \(I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}\). The finite-positive decision values, full-model least favorability, continuum discretization, localized stochastic profile bound, and negligible fallback risk remain open. A matching upper comparison is only a proposed goal on \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\). No smoothness of joint cells, conditional independence for the full class, association separation, cross-side derivative matching, oracle cutoff, or known association nuisance is imposed.

statement_notes.gap: Known-cutoff weak-fuzzy procedures do not supply the moving-location term, while sharp unknown-cutoff rates do not supply the weak causal-ratio term; this theorem derives both lower envelopes within one unchanged full model, without asserting upper-rate attainment.
statement_notes.consumer: An analyst obtains the computable lower benchmark \(F_{\alpha,s,M}(T_n)\) at every strength, the stronger maximum with \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\) where available, and the guarantee that no honest connected interval can beat the scale \(r_n\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(s\in[1,2]\). All limits below are as \(n\to\infty\). By the definitions \(T_n=n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}\) and \(\tau_n=n\kappa_n^3\), with \(\kappa_n>0\),
\[
 T_n\kappa_n^{1-1/s}
 =n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}\kappa_n^{1-1/s}
 =n\kappa_n^3
 =\tau_n.
 \tag{1}
\]

We first prove the subsequential exhaustion asserted in \(\text{def:recovery-regimes}\). For any positive sequence \((a_n)\), let \(a_\star=\liminf_n a_n\in[0,\infty]\). If \(a_\star<\infty\), then for each integer \(j\ge1\), the definition of the limit inferior gives an index \(n_j>n_{j-1}\) such that
\[
 a_\star-j^{-1}\le a_{n_j}\le a_\star+j^{-1};
\]
indeed, the lower inequality holds eventually and the upper inequality holds at some arbitrarily large index. Thus \(a_{n_j}\to a_\star\). If \(a_\star=\infty\), the definition of the limit inferior gives \(a_n\to\infty\). Applying this argument to \(a_n=\tau_n\) yields a subsequence on which \(\tau_n\to0\), \(\tau_n\to\tau\in(0,\infty)\), or \(\tau_n\to\infty\). In the third case, applying the same argument to \(\lambda_n\) along that subsequence and then passing to a further subsequence gives \(\lambda_n\to0\), \(\lambda_n\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)\), or \(\lambda_n\to\infty\). These alternatives are exactly the five components of \(\mathfrak R\) in \(\text{def:recovery-regimes}\). Their defining extended-limit conditions are pairwise incompatible, so the selected subsequence lies in exactly one component. This is a subsequential assertion; distinct subsequences of an oscillating strength sequence may lie in different components.

Suppose next that \(s=1\). The definitions give
\[
 T_n=n\kappa_n^3=\tau_n,
 \qquad
 \lambda_n=\frac{T_n}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}
 =\frac{\tau_n}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, a finite positive limit of \(\tau_n\) gives the slope face, whereas when \(\tau_n\to\infty\), the three possible extended limits of the ratio in (2) distinguish the location-entropy faces. These alternatives are nonempty. For any positive sequence \(u_n=o(n)\), set \(\kappa_n=(u_n/n)^{1/3}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with arbitrary admissible values in \((0,1/8]\) at the finitely many earlier indices. Then
\[
 \tau_n=u_n,
 \qquad
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{u_n}{1+\{\log n-\log u_n\}/3}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The choices \(u_n=(\log n)^{1/2}\), \(u_n=(\lambda/3)\log n\) for fixed \(\lambda\in(0,\infty)\), and \(u_n=(\log n)^2\) make \(\tau_n\to\infty\) while the corresponding limits of \(\lambda_n\) are respectively \(0\), \(\lambda\), and \(\infty\). A constant positive \(u_n\) gives the finite slope face.

Now suppose \(s>1\), and put \(a=1-1/s>0\). From (1) and the definition \(\lambda_n=T_n/\log(e/\kappa_n)\),
\[
 \tau_n
 =\lambda_n\kappa_n^a\log(e/\kappa_n).
 \tag{4}
\]
Assume that \(\lambda_n\) is eventually bounded. Then \(\kappa_n\to0\). Otherwise, some \(\varepsilon>0\) and a subsequence would satisfy \(\kappa_n\ge\varepsilon\), and on that subsequence
\[
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}
 \ge \frac{n\varepsilon^{2+1/s}}{\log(e/\varepsilon)}
 \longrightarrow\infty,
\]
contradicting boundedness. Moreover, \(x^a\log(e/x)\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\). To verify this directly, set \(v=x^{-1}\). For \(v\ge1\),
\[
 \log v=\int_1^v z^{-1}\,dz
 \le\int_1^v z^{a/2-1}\,dz
 \le\frac{2}{a}v^{a/2},
\]
and hence
\[
 x^a\log(e/x)
 =v^{-a}(1+\log v)
 \le v^{-a}+\frac{2}{a}v^{-a/2}longrightarrow0.
\]
Equation (4), boundedness of \(\lambda_n\), and \(\kappa_n\to0\) therefore imply \(\tau_n\to0\).

Conversely, define \(g_s(x)=x^a\log(e/x)\) for \(x\in(0,1/8]\) and set \(g_s(0)=0\). The preceding bound proves continuity at zero, while ordinary continuity holds on \((0,1/8]\); therefore
\[
 B_s:=\sup_{0\le x\le1/8}g_s(x)<\infty.
\]
Since \(g_s(\kappa_n)>0\), equation (4) yields
\[
 \lambda_n=\frac{\tau_n}{g_s(\kappa_n)}\ge\frac{\tau_n}{B_s}.
\]
Thus \(\tau_n\to\infty\) implies \(\lambda_n\to\infty\).

Cutoff recovery alone does not imply shrinking effect intervals uniformly over the declared range of smoothness exponents. Indeed, fix any \(s>1\), choose
\[
 \frac13<b<\frac{s}{2s+1},
 \qquad
 \kappa_n=\frac18 n^{-b},
 \tag{5}
\]
where the interval for \(b\) is nonempty because \(s>1\). Then \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\), and
\[
 \tau_n=8^{-3}n^{1-3b}\longrightarrow0,
\]
whereas
\[
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{8^{-(2+1/s)}n^{1-b(2+1/s)}}{\log(8e)+b\log n}
 \longrightarrow\infty
\]
because \(b<s/(2s+1)=1/(2+1/s)\). Hence \(\mathsf{CR}(s,\kappa_\bullet)\) holds by \(\text{def:recovery-regimes}\). But the definition \(r_n=\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n+1/\tau_n\}\) and \(1/\tau_n\to\infty\) give \(r_n=1\) eventually. Thus recovery does not, without the additional slope-information condition, force the effect-length scale to vanish.

The theorem \(\text{thm:integrated-and-bump-lower-frontier}\), proved under the same class \(\mathcal P_n\), states that there exists a positive constant depending only on \(s\), \(M\), and \(\alpha\) such that
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C r_n
\]
for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\). Its quantifiers do not impose any limit condition on \(\tau_n\) or \(\lambda_n\). The lower comparison therefore holds on every component of \(\mathfrak R\), including the flat and finite-positive slope faces.

For the cutoff-recovered sequence in (5), \(r_n=1\) eventually, so the same inequality gives \(\liminf_n L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C>0\). This proves, at the level of the minimax honest expected interval length rather than merely at the level of a candidate scale, that cutoff recovery alone does not imply shrinking effect intervals.

Finally, \(\text{def:profile-resolution-schedule}\) defines \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\) by first requiring membership in \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{recovered}}\) and then imposing three additional vanishing certificate conditions. Hence
\[
 \mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\subseteq\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{recovered}}.
\]
The definition poses conservative finite-grid attainment only on this certified subregime. Neither that definition nor the global lower theorem supplies an upper bound outside it, so no upper-rate or attainment conclusion has been used.

proposed.statement: For fixed \(s\in[1,2]\), \(\tau_n=T_n\kappa_n^{1-1/s}\), and every strength sequence has a subsequence in exactly one component of \(\mathfrak R\). If \(s=1\), then \(T_n=\tau_n\), so the finite and divergent location-entropy faces remain distinct according to \(\lambda_n=\tau_n/\log(e/\kappa_n)\). If fixed \(s>1\) and \(\lambda_n\) remains bounded, then \(\tau_n\to0\); if fixed \(s>1\) and \(\tau_n\to\infty\), then \(\lambda_n\to\infty\). Thus cutoff recovery \(\mathsf{CR}(s,\kappa_\bullet)\) does not by itself imply shrinking effect intervals. There exists a constant \(C>0\), depending only on \(s\), \(M\), and \(\alpha\), such that \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C r_n\) for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\); hence this lower comparison is global across all components of \(\mathfrak R\). Attainment by the conservative finite-grid procedure remains posed only on \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\subseteq\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{recovered}}\).
proposed.justification: The algebra separates global cutoff localization from the slope-induced indistinguishability that governs the causal effect label.
proposed.gap: Unknown-break papers classify location recovery, but the additional identity linking \(T_n\) and \(\tau_n\) is specific to the weak fuzzy-RD effect problem.
proposed.consumer: The partition tells an applied user which asymptotic statement is licensed by an estimated compliance strength and prevents use of a recovered-regime rate on a flat or critical face.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proved all-strength lower theorem makes the former recovered-regime-only scoping sentence stale. This replacement adds the theorem dependency, states the positive lower constant existentially rather than exposing its theorem-local name, and preserves the certified-subregime restriction on the still-unproved upper/attainment direction.
